scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Dance of Victory: Admiral Yi's Secret Weapon
This is Seungjeonmu. 1st century BC – present.
on_screen: Title card: Seungjeonmu · South Korea · 1st century BC – present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Seungjeonmu originated between the 1st century BC and 7th century AD, with early records found in Goguryeo wall paintings such as the 'Gamudo'.
It was later preserved in Tongyeong, Gyeongsangnamdo, and became synonymous with the military honors of Admiral Yi Sun-shin during the Imjin War (1592–1598).

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed to invoke victory during war and to honor Admiral Yi Sun-shin at memorial services in spring and autumn, on his birthday, and on the anniversary of his death.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance features two parts: the drum dance (Mugo) and the sword dance (Geommu).
It is characterized by '3-advances and 3-retreats' and nimble movements.
Dancers use swords to purify the space and Hansam (long sleeves) to accentuate gestures.
Watch for Sword Twirling.

Formation: Circular formation around a central drum

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is accompanied by an orchestra playing traditional pieces from the 'Yeongsan Hoisang' repertoire, specifically 'Samhyeun Dodeuri' and 'Taryeong'.
The drum, marked with a taeguk pattern, serves as a central rhythmic instrument.
Listen for the Drum, Traditional orchestra.
The music is characterized by the rhythmic beating of a large drum, intended to emulate the heartbeat of soldiers, accompanied by a traditional orchestra playing court-style melodies.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear traditional archery cloths and flower hats.
The drum dance involves four dancers in colorful attire, while the sword dance involves dancers holding swords and Hansam sleeves.
on_screen: Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Admiral Yi Sun-shin is the central figure honored by the dance, having used it to raise the morale of his troops.
The Tongyeong style is the primary preserved variant, designated as an Important Intangible Cultural Property.
It is a descendant of ancient Goguryeo dance traditions and shares origins with the Royal Court Mugo.
